**Finding: deviation (high severity) — Termination for convenience (T4C)**

**What the document does:** Section 11.1 locks in a five-year initial term with automatic one-year renewals. The only exits in Section 11.2 are uncured material breach (30-day cure) and insolvency. The 30-day notice in Section 11.1 is a non-renewal right exercisable only at a term boundary, not a convenience termination. Sections 4 and 17 contain no early-termination fee or acceleration mechanic.

**Why it fails:** Corio has no convenience exit anywhere in a five-year committed term — expressly walk-away territory under the rule, and well short of the fallback (60–90 days' notice with a fee capped at three months). On the other side of the ledger, Commerce One has no convenience right either, so nothing needs deleting, and Section 11.3 survival already protects Corio's ability to keep serving existing Customers post-termination.

**Redline (validated, ok:true):** New Section 11.3 inserted after Section 11.2 granting Corio a 30-day convenience right, in whole or in part, without penalty and with refund of prepaid fees allocable to the post-termination period, plus confirmation that Commerce One holds no mid-term convenience right. The 60–90 day fallback is offered in the negotiation comment.
